paragraphs: This paper introduces a public dataset intended to support research on safer workplaces through better labour inspections. Its motivation is practical: inspection agencies need to use their resources efficiently, and machine learning could help with decisions such as which organisations to inspect. Limited access to public data has restricted research in this area.

The Labour Inspection Checklists Dataset, or LICD, contains 63,634 inspection records from the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority, with 577 features and labels. The authors demonstrate two possible uses. The first is selecting a checklist relevant to a particular organisation. The second is predicting health, safety, and environment violations for an organisation when a particular checklist is used.

The demonstration experiments produce promising results, but also show that strong classification performance is difficult on both tasks. The contribution is therefore a research resource and a set of concrete prediction problems, rather than evidence that automated inspection decisions are already solved. By making inspection records available, the work supports further modelling and analysis connected to the goal of safe working environments.
neurips-2022-a-dataset-for-efforts-towar.tldr: LICD provides public Norwegian labour inspection data and two challenging prediction tasks to support research on safer workplaces.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to adapt an object recognition model to a new visual domain without labels from that domain. Its focus is vision transformers pretrained through self-supervised learning. This combination differs from the supervised convolutional models that much earlier domain adaptation work concentrated on, motivating an adaptation method suited to these representations.

The proposed method, PACMAC, has two stages. First, it performs additional self-supervised learning on source and target images together, aiming to learn features useful for distinguishing the task's categories. Second, it creates partial versions of target images using an attention-conditioned masking strategy. It checks whether the model's predictions remain consistent across these different partial inputs and uses that consistency to identify reliable examples for self-training.

The central idea is to make prediction stability under selective masking useful for adaptation. Partial images become a way to probe which target examples the model can handle reliably. On standard object recognition benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements over competing methods that also use vision transformers and self-supervised initialisation. Those results support the proposed adaptation procedure within the tested settings.
neurips-2022-adapting-self-supervised-vi.tldr: PACMAC adapts self-supervised vision transformers by using prediction consistency across attention-guided masked images to select self-training examples.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms repeatedly choose actions as data arrives. Classical methods can have strong performance guarantees while becoming computationally difficult when the available decision space is enormous. Oracle-efficient methods address this by delegating optimisation to an offline procedure that can find the best decision for a supplied dataset.

The paper asks whether this computational convenience can coexist with adaptation to easier environments. It considers cases where a good decision incurs little loss, as well as data drawn independently from a fixed distribution. The authors develop a framework based on follow-the-perturbed-leader algorithms that adapts to small-loss problems under a condition they call approximability. They establish that this condition holds in settings including online auctions and transductive online classification.

The authors also extend the algorithm to independent, identically distributed data and establish a best-of-both-worlds bound in the oracle-efficient setting. The significance is that an algorithm need not be judged only by its worst-case behaviour: it can exploit favourable data while retaining broader guarantees. The small-loss result specifically depends on approximability, so the stated adaptation benefit is conditional.
neurips-2022-adaptive-oracle-efficient-o.tldr: The paper develops oracle-efficient online learning algorithms that adapt to favourable environments under a stated approximability condition.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions in two steps: they first estimate understandable concepts, then use those concepts to predict an outcome. This structure is meant to make decisions easier to interpret and allows users to intervene on the intermediate concepts. However, improving outcome accuracy can come at the expense of the meaning of those concepts.

The paper examines a particular source of this tension. Training the outcome predictor on estimated concept probabilities can improve predictions compared with training on ground-truth concepts. Yet those probabilities can carry extra information beyond the intended concepts, corrupting concept predictions and weakening interventions. The authors investigate two contributing problems: a concept set that does not contain enough information and a concept predictor that is insufficiently expressive.

Their modifications address these issues and make the resulting models competitive in predictive performance with models that leak extra information through concept probabilities. At the same time, they report substantially higher concept accuracy and intervention accuracy. The finding matters because successful outcome prediction alone does not establish that a concept bottleneck remains useful as an interpretable, editable intermediate representation.
neurips-2022-addressing-leakage-in-conce.tldr: Addressing insufficient concepts and weak concept predictors improves concept bottleneck accuracy and interventions while retaining competitive outcome predictions.

paragraphs: AirfRANS is a dataset for studying learned approximations to fluid simulations around airfoils. Repeated numerical simulation can be expensive, creating a need for surrogate models when optimising physically meaningful quantities. The paper addresses a shortage of reference datasets for evaluating these data-driven models on problems connected to real physical phenomena.

The dataset covers two-dimensional, incompressible, steady-state Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes solutions in subsonic flow, with different angles of attack. These conditions define the physical setting represented by the data. Alongside the dataset, the authors introduce evaluation metrics concerning stress forces on geometry surfaces and visualisations of boundary layers. These tools focus assessment on physically relevant aspects of a prediction.

The paper also supplies deep learning baselines for four tasks: learning with abundant data, learning with scarce data, extrapolating across Reynolds numbers, and extrapolating across angles of attack. These tasks separate different generalisation demands rather than treating all prediction settings as equivalent. The contribution is a dataset and evaluation framework for examining how well learned fluid models preserve useful physical information under those demands.
neurips-2022-airfrans-high-fidelity-comp.tldr: AirfRANS provides airfoil flow simulations, physically relevant evaluation tools, and four tasks for studying learned fluid simulation surrogates.

paragraphs: Binary classifiers are often trained to minimise cross-entropy but assessed using accuracy or F1 score. These objectives measure different things, creating a gap between what training directly rewards and what evaluation ultimately values. Existing ways to optimise particular evaluation metrics can be difficult to extend to other metrics, while adversarial alternatives can be slow.

The paper proposes a shared approach for metrics built from confusion matrix entries, such as counts of correct and incorrect positive predictions. It combines a differentiable approximation to the Heaviside threshold function with a probabilistic interpretation of those entries through soft sets. This replaces the abrupt classification threshold with a formulation that supports gradient-based optimisation of the desired metric.

The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting the benefit of optimising an evaluation metric through this soft-set construction, including F1 score. They also report effective results across several experimental domains. The approach matters because it connects the training objective more directly to the criterion used to judge the classifier, while offering a common construction across confusion-matrix-based metrics.
neurips-2022-bridging-the-gap-unifying-t.tldr: A differentiable soft-set formulation lets binary classifiers train more directly toward confusion-matrix-based evaluation metrics such as F1.

paragraphs: This paper studies constrained optimisation when the objective is nonconvex and the data follows a Markov process. It focuses on the additional complication that the process's transition rule depends on the optimisation state. The resulting setting connects the evolution of the data to the optimisation problem, as can happen in reinforcement learning and strategic classification.

The authors analyse both projection-based and projection-free algorithms. The former use projections to respect constraints; the latter rely on a linear minimisation oracle. For both approaches, they establish a stochastic first-order oracle complexity of order 1/epsilon^2.5 to reach an appropriately defined epsilon-stationary point. This gives a quantitative account of the gradient information required as the requested stationarity tolerance becomes tighter.

For the projection-free approach, they additionally bound linear minimisation oracle calls by order 1/epsilon^5.5. These are guarantees about approximate stationarity in a nonconvex problem, rather than claims of finding a global optimum. The paper also demonstrates its algorithm empirically on strategic classification with neural networks, connecting the theoretical analysis to a learning problem with responsive data.
neurips-2022-constrained-stochastic-nonc.tldr: The paper establishes oracle complexity bounds for constrained nonconvex optimisation with state-dependent Markov data.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields can reconstruct a scene from images and render it from new viewpoints, but their internal representations do not naturally separate the scene into editable objects. This makes selecting and changing a particular region difficult. The paper addresses that problem by adding a semantic representation alongside the radiance field.

The authors transfer information from existing self-supervised two-dimensional image feature extractors, including CLIP-LSeg and DINO, into a three-dimensional feature field. This field is optimised in parallel with the radiance field. Once learned, it supports queries expressed as text, an image patch, or a point-and-click selection, allowing relevant parts of three-dimensional space to be identified without retraining for each query.

That semantic selection provides a route to local edits of the represented scene. The experiments show that the distilled feature fields can transfer capabilities from two-dimensional vision and language models into three-dimensional representations, producing convincing segmentation and selective editing. The contribution is the connection between queryable semantic features and a scene representation whose original structure makes object-specific editing difficult.
neurips-2022-decomposing-nerf-for-editin.tldr: Distilling image features into a 3D feature field enables query-based selection and local editing of NeRF scenes.

paragraphs: The paper considers facility location when the input changes continuously through both insertions and deletions. In this setting, maintaining a good solution is only part of the challenge. The solution should also remain stable as updates arrive, and processing those updates should be efficient enough to support an ongoing data stream.

The authors give an algorithm that combines a constant-factor approximation with polylogarithmic amortised recourse per update. The approximation guarantee controls solution quality relative to the optimum. Recourse measures changes to the maintained solution, so the second guarantee concerns stability. Because it is amortised, it controls the average amount of change over a sequence of updates rather than stating that every individual update has the same small cost.

The paper identifies this simultaneous combination of approximation quality and recourse as its first-of-its-kind contribution for the problem. An experimental analysis also supports the method's practical efficiency. Together, these results address the need to keep a changing solution useful without requiring excessive rearrangement whenever the underlying data changes.
neurips-2022-efficient-and-stable-fully-.tldr: A dynamic facility location algorithm combines constant-factor solution quality with polylogarithmic amortised changes per update.

paragraphs: This paper develops upper bounds on the generalisation error of deep neural networks trained on Markov datasets. Such data has dependence between observations, so an analysis built for independent samples does not directly describe the same setting. The authors extend an existing approach for bounding the errors of combined classifiers with independent, identically distributed data.

The central technical contribution is a set of new symmetrisation inequalities for Markov chains. These provide the probabilistic machinery needed for the extension. A key parameter is the spectral gap of the chain's infinitesimal generator, making a property of the data-generating process part of the generalisation analysis rather than treating dependence as irrelevant.

The authors also propose a simple conversion from these bounds, and other similar learning bounds, to Bayesian counterparts for both independent and Markov datasets. Further extensions cover higher-order homogeneous Markov chains, including AR and ARMA models, and mixtures of Markov data sources. The result is a broader theoretical framework for generalisation under dependent data, rather than an empirical claim about a particular trained network.
neurips-2022-generalization-error-bounds.tldr: New probability inequalities extend neural network generalisation bounds to Markov data and support Bayesian and higher-order extensions.

paragraphs: MaskTune targets shortcut learning: a model can perform a task by relying too heavily on a small number of input features, including misleading correlations. Such reliance can prevent it from learning a broader, meaningful representation. The paper proposes a simple way to push an already trained model to discover additional evidence.

During a single epoch of fine-tuning, MaskTune masks features the model has previously discovered. Removing access to that evidence forces the model to explore other features. The method does not require annotations identifying spurious features or labels indicating dataset subgroups. This is useful because those extra annotations are precisely the information that some earlier shortcut-mitigation approaches depend on.

Experiments on biased MNIST, CelebA, Waterbirds, and ImageNet-9L show effectiveness on tasks affected by spurious correlations. The authors also evaluate selective classification, where a classifier can reject a prediction, and report performance that matches or exceeds competing methods. These empirical results support masking as a lightweight fine-tuning strategy for reducing excessive dependence on a limited feature set.
neurips-2022-masktune-mitigating-spuriou.tldr: MaskTune uses one epoch of feature-masking fine-tuning to reduce shortcut reliance without requiring spurious-feature or subgroup annotations.

paragraphs: MCVD brings several video synthesis tasks into one conditional diffusion framework. Instead of treating future prediction, past prediction, interpolation, and unconditional generation as separate modelling problems, it changes which surrounding frames are available to the same model. The motivation is to improve video synthesis while broadening the tasks a single model can handle.

During training, the method randomly and independently hides the past conditioning frames or the future conditioning frames. With only past frames available, it predicts forward; with only future frames available, it predicts backward. Hiding both gives unconditional generation, while retaining both supports interpolation. The model learns to denoise video content under these different patterns of available context.

The architecture uses non-recurrent two-dimensional convolutions and processes blocks of frames. Generating successive blocks autoregressively allows videos of arbitrary length. The authors report high-quality frames across diverse videos and state-of-the-art results on standard prediction and interpolation benchmarks. Reported training takes one to twelve days using at most four GPUs, providing a concrete computational context for those experimental results.
neurips-2022-mcvd-masked-conditional-vid.tldr: MCVD uses random masking of past and future conditioning frames to train one diffusion model for multiple video synthesis tasks.

paragraphs: Parametric partial differential equations describe families of problems whose physical parameters, boundary conditions, or domain shapes can vary. Learning-based solvers face a tradeoff: some avoid labelled solution data and meshes but require fresh training for each instance, while others predict solutions quickly after training on many paired simulations, often using a predefined mesh.

The proposed Meta-Auto-Decoder, or MAD, is an unsupervised, mesh-free method designed for quick adaptation of a pretrained model to individual equation instances. It implicitly represents PDE parameters as latent vectors, including potentially heterogeneous kinds of parameters. This gives the pretrained model a compact way to accommodate variations across the equation family while still adapting to a particular instance.

The authors interpret MAD through manifold learning in infinite-dimensional spaces, providing a geometric perspective on its representation of solutions. Numerical experiments show faster convergence than other deep learning approaches without a loss of accuracy. The stated benefit is faster adaptation and convergence, connecting reusable learning across a family of PDEs with a solver that does not require a predefined mesh or paired solution supervision.
neurips-2022-meta-auto-decoder-for-solvi.tldr: MAD represents PDE variations through latent vectors to enable fast, unsupervised, mesh-free adaptation of a pretrained solver.

paragraphs: A model that predicts observed transitions accurately does not necessarily help an agent make better decisions. An agent may exploit the few places where a generally accurate model is wrong, while avoiding the errors of a less accurate one. This paper addresses the resulting mismatch between training a dynamics model for prediction accuracy and using it to obtain high-return policies.

The authors propose one objective for jointly training the model and policy: a lower bound on expected return that updates to either component increase. They describe the bound as globally valid and efficiently estimable in continuous settings, with a version becoming tight under certain assumptions. Its optimisation resembles adversarial learning: a classifier distinguishes real from model-generated transitions, the model makes transitions look realistic, and the policy avoids states with unrealistic predictions.

Numerical simulations show reward-maximising policies and model dynamics that can assist exploration. A deep reinforcement learning algorithm loosely based on the bound performs competitively with previous model-based methods and better on certain difficult exploration tasks. These experiments support the shared objective while distinguishing the practical algorithm from exact optimisation of the theoretical bound.
neurips-2022-mismatched-no-more-joint-mo.tldr: A shared lower-bound objective aligns dynamics-model and policy training with expected return rather than prediction accuracy alone.

paragraphs: MoVQ addresses repeated visual artifacts in two-stage image generators that represent image patches using discrete codes. Similar patches can receive the same code, and existing decoders can produce repeated patterns in nearby regions as a result. The paper aims to retain this compact representation while improving the images reconstructed from it.

Its central change is spatially conditional normalization, which modulates the quantized vectors with information that varies across image locations. This gives the decoder spatial variation to work with even when patches share a discrete index. The intended effect is to encourage more photorealistic images by enriching the information available during decoding.

The method also uses multichannel quantization to expand how discrete codes can be recombined without increasing model or codebook cost. For the second stage, it adopts MaskGIT to learn the distribution of tokens in the compressed representation. The abstract describes this token-generation approach as much faster than conventional autoregressive modeling.

Experiments on two benchmark datasets report substantially improved reconstruction quality and high-fidelity image generation. These findings support the value of modulating quantized representations: the reported gains concern both recovering an image from its compressed codes and producing images through the full generative process.
neurips-2022-movq-modulating-quantized-v.tldr: MoVQ enriches discrete image codes with spatial variation to reduce repeated artifacts and improve reconstruction and generation quality.

paragraphs: Deep networks can memorise incorrect training labels, hurting their ability to generalise. Noise Attention Learning aims to reduce that effect by automatically adjusting how much individual examples influence learning. Its goal is to distinguish misleading examples from useful ones without allowing noisy labels to dominate the training process.

The method adds an attention branch that produces weights from each sample's representation. This branch learns to separate samples according to the predictive information in those representations. A corresponding loss incorporates the weights while preserving the original learning direction. The theoretical analysis explains the mechanism as dynamic scaling of sample gradients, reducing the influence of examples assigned lower attention.

Empirically, most incorrectly labelled examples receive substantially lower weights than clean examples. This is a qualified separation result, rather than a claim that every noisy label is identified. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with simulated noise, plus ANIMAL-10N, Clothing1M, and Webvision with real-world noise, show improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support gradient scaling as a way to limit memorisation of mislabeled data.
neurips-2022-noise-attention-learning-en.tldr: Noise Attention Learning scales sample gradients with learned attention weights to reduce memorisation of incorrect labels.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the transition between two different training behaviours in shallow neural networks. Overparameterised networks can achieve global convergence under gradient descent despite nonconvex objectives, whereas narrow networks tend to become trapped in local minima that generalise poorly. The authors study how these regimes connect in a high-dimensional setting.

The analysis focuses on Gaussian data and the interaction among learning rate, training time scale, and the number of hidden units during stochastic gradient descent. Considering these quantities together helps frame the crossover as a question about training dynamics, rather than network width in isolation. The work also examines the connection between the mean-field or hydrodynamic regime and the earlier Saad–Solla approach.

The authors extend a deterministic description of high-dimensional stochastic gradient descent drawn from statistical physics and provide rigorous convergence rates for that description. The contribution is a theoretical account linking different regimes of shallow-network learning. Its stated Gaussian-data focus is part of the setting in which the analysis is developed, so the results should be understood within that scope.
neurips-2022-phase-diagram-of-stochastic.tldr: The paper analyses how width, learning rate, and time scale shape high-dimensional SGD dynamics in shallow networks with Gaussian data.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can learn physical behaviour described by partial differential equations, but reliable prediction requires handling boundary conditions properly. A second difficulty arises over long time intervals: physical interactions can become global even though graph networks typically exchange information locally. This paper addresses both issues in a learned PDE solver.

The proposed physics-embedded neural network incorporates boundary conditions and uses an implicit method to predict states farther into the future. It is built on an E(n)-equivariant graph neural network, connecting the architecture to geometric structure. The authors report that this design supports strong generalisation across different shapes, which matters for physical problems posed on varying computational domains.

Experiments show the model learning flow phenomena in complex geometries. In the reported comparisons, it offers a better balance of speed and accuracy than both a well-optimised classical solver and a state-of-the-art machine learning model. The result supports combining boundary-condition handling, implicit prediction, and geometric structure as a route toward reliable graph-based solvers in the tested flow settings.
neurips-2022-physics-embedded-neural-net.tldr: Physics-embedded graph networks combine boundary-condition handling and implicit prediction to improve the speed–accuracy tradeoff for learned flow simulation.

paragraphs: PointNeXt revisits PointNet++ to examine why newer point-cloud networks outperform it. The authors find that a large share of the improvement comes from training choices and model size, rather than architectural changes alone. This motivates a systematic study of augmentation, optimisation, and scaling before introducing a revised architecture.

Improved training raises PointNet++ accuracy on ScanObjectNN from 77.9% to 86.1% without changing its architecture, surpassing PointMLP in that comparison. The authors then add inverted residual bottlenecks and separable multilayer perceptrons to support efficient scaling. The resulting PointNeXt family is designed to expand flexibly while retaining an effective foundation from PointNet++.

PointNeXt reaches 87.7% overall accuracy on ScanObjectNN and is reported to run inference ten times faster than PointMLP. On S3DIS semantic segmentation, it achieves 74.9% mean intersection over union under six-fold cross-validation, outperforming Point Transformer. These results show why training procedures and scale deserve attention when assessing architectural progress, while also demonstrating gains from the proposed scalable design.
neurips-2022-pointnext-revisiting-pointn.tldr: PointNeXt combines stronger PointNet++ training with efficient architectural scaling to improve point-cloud classification and segmentation.

paragraphs: The paper develops quantum algorithms for sampling distributions proportional to exp(-f(x)), where f is convex, and estimating the integral that normalises those distributions. These log-concave problems arise across machine learning, statistics, and physics. The analysis measures efficiency through query complexity and its dependence on dimension, conditioning, and requested accuracy.

One family uses underdamped Langevin diffusion. Its dependence on condition number and dimension matches analogous classical algorithms that request gradients, even though the quantum algorithms request only function evaluations. For normalising constants, this family also achieves a quadratic improvement in dependence on multiplicative error. The comparison therefore concerns both how much information is requested and how many queries are needed.

A second family uses quantum Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithms, quantum Monte Carlo methods, and quantum walks. The authors establish polynomial query-complexity improvements over the best known classical algorithms in the stated parameters. They also prove a quantum lower bound for normalising-constant estimation that nearly matches their algorithms' dependence on accuracy. This near-optimality concerns that error dependence specifically, rather than every aspect of computational cost.
neurips-2022-quantum-algorithms-for-samp.tldr: Quantum sampling and integration algorithms improve query complexity for log-concave distributions, with nearly optimal accuracy dependence for normalising constants.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimisation uses a surrogate model to decide which inputs of an unknown objective to evaluate. Gaussian-process surrogates can struggle with categorical, high-dimensional, or image inputs, motivating neural alternatives. However, existing theoretically supported neural approaches can require inversion of an extremely large parameter matrix and restrict evaluations to a sequential setting.

The paper introduces two batch Thompson-sampling algorithms, STO-BNTS and STO-BNTS-Linear. Selecting a query involves training a neural network or a linear model and then maximising that trained model. The authors connect this procedure to sampling from a Gaussian-process posterior with a neural tangent kernel. That connection preserves the Thompson-sampling interpretation while avoiding the large matrix inversion.

The authors derive regret upper bounds for batch evaluations and establish asymptotically no-regret behaviour under certain conditions. This conditional guarantee describes how performance compares with the best choices over time, rather than ensuring every selected query is optimal. Experiments in automated machine learning and reinforcement learning support the algorithms' practical effectiveness, linking their computational construction to applications that benefit from batch evaluation.
neurips-2022-sample-then-optimize-batch-.tldr: Two neural Thompson-sampling algorithms enable batch optimisation without large parameter-matrix inversion and provide conditional no-regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware training seeks model parameters in flatter regions of the loss landscape, an approach associated with better generalisation. Existing Sharpness-Aware Minimisation methods approximate sharpness at roughly twice the computational cost of their base optimiser. This paper proposes SAF, a method intended to obtain similar benefits with almost no additional computation.

SAF replaces the usual sharpness measure with a trajectory loss based on the KL divergence between predictions made using current and past model weights. This loss captures how training loss changes along the sequence of parameter updates. The method discourages sudden loss drops associated with sharp local minima, using the model's training trajectory to guide it toward a flatter solution.

The authors describe minimising this trajectory loss as ensuring convergence to a flat minimum with improved generalisation. Their extensive empirical results show sharpness reduction similar to SAM and better ImageNet results while keeping computational cost essentially at that of the base optimiser. The practical contribution is a different signal for sharpness-aware learning that avoids the usual twofold training overhead.
neurips-2022-sharpness-aware-training-fo.tldr: SAF uses changes in model predictions along training to encourage flat minima at nearly the computational cost of the base optimiser.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference estimates plausible model parameters by comparing observations with outputs from a stochastic simulator. Sequential methods improve simulation efficiency by repeatedly adapting the distribution used to generate new simulations. In practice, however, those adaptations can introduce difficult optimisation problems, and checking the resulting inference can itself be challenging.

The paper proposes Truncated Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation, or TSNPE. It uses truncated proposal distributions during sequential inference to sidestep optimisation difficulties encountered by alternative approaches. It also supports efficient coverage tests that scale to models with many parameters. This makes diagnostic assessment part of the method's contribution alongside the posterior estimation procedure.

On established benchmarks, TSNPE performs comparably to previous methods. The authors then apply it to two challenging neuroscience problems, obtaining posterior distributions where earlier methods fail. These findings support the method's stated efficiency, accuracy, and robustness in the evaluated settings. Its significance is the combination of sequential simulation efficiency with a more manageable optimisation procedure and scalable tools for checking inference quality.
neurips-2022-truncated-proposals-for-sca.tldr: TSNPE uses truncated proposals to simplify sequential simulation-based inference and enable scalable coverage testing.

paragraphs: Detecting human–object interactions in video requires representing both what appears in each frame and how related content extends through time. The paper proposes TUTOR, a vision transformer that learns tubelet tokens as compact representations of this spatial and temporal information. These tokens organise the video around semantically related content.

TUTOR forms tubelet tokens by gathering and linking related image-patch tokens across space and time. A selective attention mechanism reduces redundant dependencies, making the resulting representation compact. At the same time, grouping and linking allow a token to align with a semantic instance such as a person or object. The design therefore aims to preserve interaction-relevant information while reducing unnecessary relationships between tokens.

Experiments support both effectiveness and efficiency. The authors report a 16.14% relative gain in mean average precision on VidHOI, a two-point improvement on CAD-120, and a fourfold speedup. The relative VidHOI gain is distinct from an absolute percentage-point increase. Together, the reported results support learned tubelet representations as a useful way to structure video for interaction detection.
neurips-2022-video-based-human-object-in.tldr: TUTOR groups related video patches into tubelet tokens, improving human–object interaction detection accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, policy optimisation and dynamics-model learning depend on each other. Updating the model can therefore change the foundation on which the policy was improved. The paper argues that existing discrepancy bounds often neglect these model shifts, leaving associated algorithms vulnerable to performance drops after drastic model updates.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for non-decreasing performance and derive bounds that explicitly relate model changes to improvement. These motivate a constrained lower-bound optimisation problem. An additional example shows that varying the amount of exploration used for model learning can benefit eventual returns, suggesting that model updates should respond to the learning process rather than follow an inflexible schedule.

The resulting algorithm, Constrained Model-shift Lower-bound Optimization, uses an event-triggered mechanism to decide when to update the model. Experiments show it outperforming other state-of-the-art methods and improving results with several policy optimisation methods. The work connects update timing to theoretical control of model shifts, while the reported practical benefits come from the evaluated algorithm and experimental settings.
neurips-2022-when-to-update-your-model-c.tldr: CMLO uses theory about model shifts to trigger dynamics-model updates and improve model-based reinforcement learning.
